sources.citation: Suter, Edgar. 2018. Comparative Morphology of the Huon Peninsula Languages (Papua New Guinea). PhD dissertation, Universität zu Köln. viii+331 pp. (Glottolog ref 577703)
sources.note: Comparative morphology only ('the comparative phonology still awaits completion', Preface). p. 7: 'None of the three languages of this family [Dallman] has been the object of an in-depth study... McElhanon as well as myself collected morphological and lexical data on Nomu'; p. 58: Nomu data = McElhanon's 1968 survey + Suter's 1996 object-verb elicitation. The only stress/accent remarks are historical-comparative conjectures about Proto-Western-Huon suffixes being unstressed (text lines 5804-5809) and Selepet/Kâte word accent (lines 7363-7368, p. 250); nothing on Nomu word stress.

sources.citation: Smith, Geoffrey P. 1988. Morobe counting systems. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 26 (PL A-76), 1-132. (Glottolog ref 8921; ANU Open Research hdl 1885/253560)
sources.note: §56 Nomu (p. 83): numerals 1-20 from a high-school student (wetku, okop, okop so wetku, mete wetku...). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. 1984. A linguistic field guide to the Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics D-57. (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/145233)
sources.note: Village gazetteer (Ezanko, Gitukia, Sikikia listed as Nomu villages). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. 1975. North-Eastern Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 1 (PL C-38), 527-567. (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/252970)
sources.note: Survey/classification chapter. §2.8.1.3.3.3 Nomu (WH-10), p. 535: pop. 810; 'In 1968 informants indicated to the present writer that the Nomu language became extinct about 1900. Data collected at that time revealed ONO roots with NOMU affixation. More recent comments, however, indicate that there may yet be some Nomu speakers alive.' No stress statement (0 hits).

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. 1973. Towards a typology of the Finisterre-Huon languages, New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics B-22. Canberra: ANU. viii+80 pp. (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/145136)

sources.note: Ch. 1 Phonology (pp. 5-7: phonemes, syllable structure, morphophonemics) compares ten representative languages (Rawa, Wantoat, Uri, Kewieng, Kube, Kâte, Kovai, Nabak, Selepet,...), not Nomu; Nomu appears only in the classification list (p. vii). No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the book (de-spaced scanned grep: 0 hits).

sources.citation: Hooley, B. A. & K. A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Morobe District, New Guinea. In Wurm & Laycock (eds), Pacific linguistic studies in honour of Arthur Capell (PL C-13), 1065-1094. (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/253805)
sources.note: Lexicostatistical classification. Nomu: 50% cognate with Ono, non-basic vocabulary largely replaced by Ono forms; 'Informants indicate that the aboriginal speakers of Nomu died out about the time of initial European contact.' Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. & C. L. Voorhoeve. 1970. The Trans-New Guinea Phylum: explorations in deep-level genetic relationships. Pacific Linguistics B-16. (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/146444)
sources.note: Source of the Nomu wordlist used by TransNewGuinea.org/Rosetta; Nomu appears only in the classification list (Western Huon Family e.). No stress marking, no stress statement.
